walkthroughs.body_html:
Working as a Physicist — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Working as a Physicist brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Working as a Physicist.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Is a reproducible result the same as a repeatable one?
options: No — reproducible just means it was published twice.
No — repeatable means the same experimenter and method agree; reproducible means others, with different methods or labs, agree.
No — validity only applies to surveys.
Yes — the two words are interchangeable.

mcqs.q: Does using a precise instrument guarantee a valid experiment?
options: Yes — better equipment automatically makes the conclusion valid.
No — validity depends on controlling variables so the experiment tests the intended relationship.
No — validity only applies to surveys.
No — reproducible just means it was published twice.

mcqs.q: Can new evidence overturn a well-established theory?
options: Yes — scientific knowledge is provisional and is revised when reliable conflicting evidence appears.
No — validity only applies to surveys.
No — once proven, theories become permanent facts.
Yes — but only after a hundred years have passed.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Repeatability”?
options: The international system of units; base units include the metre, kilogram, second and ampere.
Making order-of-magnitude judgements of physical quantities to check whether answers are reasonable.
Standard multipliers attached to units, such as kilo (10³), mega (10⁶), milli (10⁻³) and micro (10⁻⁶).
A measurement is repeatable if the same experimenter, using the same method and equipment, obtains similar results.

options: Making order-of-magnitude judgements of physical quantities to check whether answers are reasonable.

Scrutiny of scientific findings by other experts before publication, helping to validate claims.
